author: Douglas Walton
key_works: Argumentation Schemes (2008, with Reed and Macagno)
distinctive_feature: Identifies argumentation as primarily presumptive (defeasible, contextually sufficient) rather than formally valid, and provides a catalog of argument patterns each with its own set of critical questions for evaluation.
description: Douglas Walton's argumentation schemes framework addresses a fundamental gap in classical logic's account of everyday reasoning. Formal logic deals with arguments that are valid or invalid — where valid means the conclusion cannot be false if the premises are true. But almost all real-world reasoning is not formally valid in this sense. We regularly accept arguments that could be wrong, that rest on incomplete evidence, and that would be revised in light of new information. Walton calls these presumptive arguments: arguments that are reasonable to accept as working hypotheses until specific defeating conditions are identified. Argumentation schemes are the recurring patterns — the templates — that presumptive arguments follow. Each scheme has associated critical questions: the specific probing questions that, if answered negatively, defeat the scheme's presumption.
dewey_connection: Walton's presumptive reasoning corresponds to Dewey's account of hypothesis formation and evaluation in reflective inquiry. Dewey understood that inquiry typically proceeds not through formal deduction but through working hypotheses held provisionally — 'good enough to act on, pending further inquiry.' Argumentation schemes give this Deweyan insight structural form: each scheme specifies what kind of evidence is sufficient to provisionally accept a claim, and what would defeat that acceptance.

core_concepts.presumptive_reasoning: Reasoning that is defeasible — correct in normal circumstances but subject to defeat when exceptional circumstances apply. Most real-world argumentation is presumptive, not formally valid.
core_concepts.defeasibility: A property of arguments: an argument is defeasible if its conclusion can be withdrawn in light of new information without logical contradiction. Defeasible arguments are not weak — they are the appropriate form for reasoning under incomplete information.
core_concepts.critical_questions: Each argumentation scheme has a set of associated critical questions — the specific challenges that, when raised and unanswered, defeat the presumption of the argument. Critical questions are not rhetorical; they identify genuine defeating conditions built into the structure of the scheme.

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Expert Opinion
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: Expert E claims that proposition P is true in domain D. Therefore, P is (presumably) true.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: The testimony of domain experts on matters within their expertise is generally reliable
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: When a claim requires specialized knowledge beyond general reasoning and the expert has relevant credentials and track record
critical_questions: Is E a genuine expert in the relevant domain (not merely a celebrity or authority-figure)?
Is the claim within E's actual area of expertise?
Is E reliable and trustworthy — not biased by conflicts of interest?
Is the claim actually consistent with E's testimony, or has it been misrepresented?
Do other experts in the same domain agree, or is this a contested expert opinion?
What is the current state of evidence in this domain — is this an area of genuine consensus?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Citing an expert in one domain to support claims in a different domain (domain transfer fallacy). Treating any single expert opinion as definitive regardless of consensus.

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Analogy
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: Case C1 has property P. Case C2 is relevantly similar to C1 in important respects. Therefore, C2 (presumably) also has property P.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: Similar cases in relevant respects will have similar relevant properties
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: When a new case lacks direct evidence but has strong structural similarities to well-understood cases
critical_questions: Are C1 and C2 genuinely similar in the respects relevant to property P?
Are there relevant differences between C1 and C2 that might defeat the analogy?
Are there other cases analogous to C2 but lacking property P?
Is the analogy the main source of evidence or merely illustrative?
Could the analogy break down in important ways under the specific conditions of C2?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Ignoring disanalogies, treating superficial similarity as deep similarity, using multiple analogies without noticing they conflict.

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Cause to Effect
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: Cause C has been observed. C leads to effect E in cases like this. Therefore, E (presumably) will occur.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: Known causal relationships can be projected to similar cases
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: When predicting consequences of actions, policies, or events based on known causal mechanisms
critical_questions: Is the causal connection between C and E well established, or merely assumed?
Are the conditions in this case sufficiently similar to past cases for the causal relationship to hold?
Could other factors prevent E from occurring despite C?
Could C produce multiple effects, some of which conflict?
Is the causal mechanism understood, or only the correlation?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Confusing correlation with causation, ignoring confounding factors, treating all causal relationships as deterministic.

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Sign
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: Evidence E is observed. E is typically a sign of proposition P. Therefore, P is (presumably) true.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: Reliable signs (symptoms, indicators, markers) are sufficient evidence for their signified conditions
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: Diagnostic reasoning — inferring from observable evidence to underlying states, conditions, or causes
critical_questions: Is E a reliable sign of P, or merely a possible sign?
Are there alternative explanations for E that do not involve P?
What is the base rate of P — how often does E occur without P?
Are there other signs present that confirm or disconfirm P?
Could E be misleading or artificially produced?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Diagnostic overconfidence — treating a single sign as definitive without considering alternatives. Ignoring base rate (how common is what we're diagnosing?).

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Consequences (Practical Reasoning)
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: Action A would produce desirable consequence C (or avoid undesirable consequence D). Therefore, A should (presumably) be done.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: Actions that produce good consequences or prevent bad ones are presumptively justified
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: Practical decision-making where justification proceeds from predicted consequences
critical_questions: Will A actually produce C (is the causal claim accurate)?
Is C genuinely desirable — from whose perspective?
Are there unintended negative consequences of A that should be weighed?
Are there alternative actions that would produce the same or better consequences at lower cost?
Are there values or principles that override consequentialist justification in this case?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Slippery slope without specifying the mechanism, ignoring unintended consequences, treating all values as reducible to consequences.

major_argumentation_schemes.name: Argument from Popular Opinion
major_argumentation_schemes.scheme_structure: The majority of people in population P believe proposition Q. Therefore, Q is (presumably) true/acceptable.
major_argumentation_schemes.presumption: Widespread belief in a population with relevant experience provides some evidence for the believed proposition
major_argumentation_schemes.when_appropriate: Social norms, customary practices, and widely shared experiential claims where distributed experience provides evidence
critical_questions: Is the population P one with relevant experience or competence regarding Q?
Does the majority actually hold this belief, or is it being exaggerated?
Could the majority belief be the result of misinformation, propaganda, or shared error?
Is Q the kind of claim where popular belief is evidentially relevant (factual) or irrelevant (moral)?
Has the popular belief been tested against evidence?
major_argumentation_schemes.common_misuse: Ad Populum — treating popularity as evidence for truth regardless of whether the majority has relevant experience or has been subject to systematic misinformation.

the_walton_innovation.description: Walton's key contribution is recognizing that these schemes are not fallacies — they are legitimate forms of reasoning that become fallacious only when their critical questions cannot be satisfactorily answered. Argument from Expert Opinion is not inherently a fallacy (Appeal to Authority). It is a valid presumptive argument form that becomes fallacious when the expert conditions fail.
the_walton_innovation.implication: Most real-world CT instruction correctly identifies fallacious uses of these schemes (ad populum, appeal to authority, slippery slope) but fails to identify the legitimate, non-fallacious uses. Walton provides the framework for distinguishing them: ask the scheme's critical questions. If they can be answered, the argument is reasonable. If not, it's a fallacy.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Argument from authority (expert opinion) is always a fallacy.
common_misconceptions.correction: Argument from expert opinion is a legitimate presumptive argument form when the expert conditions are met. Experts exist precisely so their testimony can be reasonably accepted without independent verification. The question is whether the conditions hold.
common_misconceptions.practical_implication: When evaluating expert citations, apply the six critical questions for Argument from Expert Opinion rather than dismissing the appeal as inherently fallacious.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Slippery slope arguments are always fallacious.
common_misconceptions.correction: Slippery slope is a legitimate argument from consequences when the causal mechanism for the slide is specified and plausible. It becomes the slippery slope fallacy when the mechanism is assumed without evidence.
common_misconceptions.practical_implication: When confronting a slippery slope argument, ask: 'What specific mechanism explains why the slide would occur?' A satisfactory answer makes it a legitimate causal argument; no answer makes it a fallacy.

app_usage.primary_use: Providing a structured approach to evaluating real-world arguments that operate through presumptive reasoning
app_usage.exercise_integration: Argumentation scheme identification and critical question application are features of advanced argument analysis exercises. The Toulmin framework provides the argument structure; Walton's schemes identify the type of reasoning being used; critical questions provide the specific probing tools.
app_usage.cross_reference: Compare with Toulmin Argument Model (argument structure), Logical Fallacies (fallacious uses of schemes), Ennis Framework (critical disposition to apply critical questions).
app_usage.key_insight_for_learners: Most real arguments you encounter are presumptive, not formally valid. The question is not 'Is this argument logically valid?' but 'Which scheme is this argument using, and are its critical questions satisfactorily answered?'

historical_origin.aristotelian_roots: Walton's argumentation schemes are the modern elaboration of a problem Aristotle identified in his 'Topics' and 'Rhetoric': that most practical reasoning is not demonstrative (valid deduction from certain premises) but dialectical (reasonable inference from probable premises, subject to defeat). Aristotle's 'Topics' was precisely a catalog of argument forms (topoi) for use in dialectical debate — the direct ancestor of Walton's scheme catalog. The two-and-a-half millennia between Aristotle and Walton saw formal logic develop powerfully but at the cost of relegating dialectical reasoning to a second-class status. Walton's project was to restore philosophical rigor to the study of the arguments that actually govern real-world reasoning.
historical_origin.informal_logic_movement: Walton's work emerged from the informal logic movement of the 1970s and 1980s, pioneered by scholars including Ralph Johnson, J. Anthony Blair, and Michael Scriven, who argued that formal deductive logic was insufficient for evaluating the arguments people actually make in everyday life, politics, law, science, and medicine. The informal logic movement produced the first generation of CT textbooks that moved beyond syllogisms to analyze argument quality in natural language. Walton was a central figure in this movement, publishing extensively on fallacies, argument structure, and dialectical theory from the 1970s onward.
historical_origin.walton_s_career: Douglas Walton, a philosopher at the University of Windsor and later the University of Winnipeg, spent his career of over forty years developing argumentation theory as a rigorous academic discipline. His 1996 book 'Argumentation Schemes for Presumptive Reasoning' presented the first systematic catalog of presumptive schemes with their critical questions. His subsequent collaboration with Chris Reed and Fabrizio Macagno, 'Argumentation Schemes' (2008), expanded the catalog to over sixty schemes and became the authoritative reference in the field. Walton was one of the most prolific argumentation theorists of the twentieth century, with over fifty books on topics including fallacy theory, legal reasoning, informal logic, and the ethics of argumentation.
historical_origin.artificial_intelligence_connection: Walton's argumentation schemes have had significant impact beyond philosophy in the field of argumentation mining and computational argumentation — the attempt to automatically identify, extract, and evaluate arguments in text. His formalized scheme structures and critical questions are well-suited to computational implementation, and the schemes have been incorporated into AI reasoning systems, legal decision-support tools, and natural language processing research. This practical impact in AI research is unusual for philosophical work and reflects the rigor and precision of Walton's formalism.

teaching_applications.overview: Walton's schemes transform argument evaluation from a binary fallacy/non-fallacy judgment into a structured diagnostic procedure: identify the scheme, apply the critical questions, determine whether the conditions for legitimate use are met. This nuanced approach develops genuine evaluative competence rather than pattern-matching for named fallacies.

scheme_identification_exercise.description: Present students with a collection of real arguments from news, politics, advertising, and academic papers. Students identify which scheme each argument uses and state the specific critical questions that apply.
implementation: Select 8-10 brief argument samples across diverse domains.
Students classify each by scheme: Expert Opinion? Analogy? Cause-to-Effect? Popular Opinion? Sign? Consequences?
For each identified scheme, students list the 4-6 critical questions that apply and answer each one based on the information available.
Students distinguish: Which arguments are legitimate uses of their scheme? Which are fallacious uses (i.e., which critical questions are unanswerable)?
scheme_identification_exercise.pedagogical_value: This exercise builds the core skill Walton's framework develops: distinguishing legitimate from fallacious uses of the same argument form. Most students initially treat all appeals to authority as fallacies; this exercise reveals that some are legitimate and others are not — and that the difference can be specified precisely.

critical_questions_deep_dive.description: Work through a single important argument in detail, applying all of one scheme's critical questions systematically and documenting the quality of the answers.
critical_questions_deep_dive.implementation: Select a significant claim in a policy or scientific debate. Identify the primary scheme. For each critical question: (1) What evidence would answer this question? (2) Is that evidence available? (3) Is the answer satisfactory or unsatisfactory? (4) If unsatisfactory, does it defeat the argument or merely weaken it?
critical_questions_deep_dive.example: Take a medical recommendation citing expert consensus. Apply all six critical questions for Argument from Expert Opinion. Is the 'consensus' genuine or manufactured? Is the domain one where expert judgment is reliable? What does the answer tell you about how confidently the recommendation should be accepted?

fallacy_reclassification_exercise.description: Present classic informal fallacy examples and ask students to reanalyze them using Walton's scheme framework. The goal is to see that many 'fallacies' are fallacious uses of legitimate schemes — not inherently invalid argument forms.
examples: 'Ad hominem' (Attack on the Person): when is it the Ad Hominem fallacy vs. a legitimate challenge to an arguer's credibility in the context of Argument from Expert Opinion?
'Appeal to Authority': when is citing an expert fallacious (domain transfer, bias, minority view) vs. legitimate (genuine expertise, unbiased, consensus)?
'Slippery Slope': when is the causal chain unjustified (fallacy) vs. specified and plausible (legitimate Argument from Consequences)?
fallacy_reclassification_exercise.insight: This exercise is transformative for students who have learned to dismiss entire argument categories as fallacies: it replaces a binary fallacy/non-fallacy judgment with a structured diagnostic procedure.

real_world_application.description: Require students to apply Walton's scheme analysis to an argument they encounter in their professional or academic domain — a case where the scheme analysis produces an actionable conclusion about whether to accept, reject, or seek more information.
real_world_application.output: A structured analysis identifying: the scheme used, each critical question and its answer, the overall conclusion about whether the argument's presumption is defeated or sustained, and what action is warranted.

scheme_recognition: When I encounter an argument, do I identify what type of reasoning it is using (scheme identification) before evaluating it — or do I go straight to 'do I agree with this?'
Can I distinguish an Argument from Expert Opinion from an ad populum appeal, and specify exactly where the critical questions for each differ?
When I use an argument from analogy myself, do I explicitly check for relevant disanalogies that could defeat it?
Do I recognize causal reasoning as presumptive — subject to defeat by alternative explanations and confounding factors — or do I treat confirmed causal mechanisms as certain?
critical_question_application: When I accept an expert opinion, have I applied at least the first three critical questions (domain relevance, bias, consensus) or am I accepting based on credentialing alone?
When I accept or make an analogical argument, have I actively looked for relevant differences, not just relevant similarities?
When I encounter a slippery slope argument, do I ask for the specific causal mechanism, or do I accept or reject it based on whether I like the conclusion?
In my most recent significant decision based on consequentialist reasoning, did I explicitly consider alternative actions and unintended negative consequences?
legitimate_vs_fallacious_distinction: Am I applying Walton's insight — that these schemes are presumptively legitimate unless the critical questions are unsatisfied — or am I treating certain argument forms as inherently suspicious regardless of context?

When I identify a potential fallacy in an argument, can I specify which critical question is being violated and why the answer to it is inadequate — or am I pattern-matching to a fallacy name without the diagnostic precision?

toulmin_argument_model.description: The Toulmin model provides the structural skeleton of arguments (Claim, Data, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal); Walton's schemes identify the type of reasoning that constitutes the Warrant. Where Toulmin asks 'What licenses this move from Data to Claim?', Walton's schemes specify the answer: 'This is licensed by Expert Opinion / Analogy / Cause-to-Effect / etc.' Walton's critical questions are then the specific challenges to the Warrant of each scheme type.
toulmin_argument_model.combined_use: Use Toulmin to map an argument's structural components; use Walton to classify the type of reasoning used in the Warrant and apply the appropriate critical questions. The two frameworks operate at different levels of analysis that complement each other.

logical_fallacies_framework.description: Walton's most important contribution to the Logical Fallacies tradition is his demonstration that most named informal fallacies are not inherently fallacious but are fallacious uses of legitimate argumentation schemes. Ad Hominem is a fallacious use of credibility-based challenges; Appeal to Authority is a fallacious use of Argument from Expert Opinion; Slippery Slope is a fallacious use of Argument from Consequences. Walton's framework transforms the fallacy inventory from a list of bad argument forms into a diagnostic system: each fallacy name now specifies which critical questions are being violated.
logical_fallacies_framework.key_insight: The Logical Fallacies framework teaches students what to avoid; Walton's framework teaches students to distinguish when the same argument form is legitimate vs. fallacious — a higher-order skill that reduces false positives in fallacy detection.

browne_keeley.description: Browne and Keeley's 10 Questions provide a domain-general argument evaluation protocol; Walton's schemes provide scheme-specific critical questions that are more targeted and powerful once the scheme has been identified. Browne-Keeley's Question 7 (evidence quality) and Question 8 (alternative explanations) are generic versions of the more specific critical questions Walton's schemes prescribe for each argument type.
browne_keeley.combined_use: Use Browne-Keeley as the default protocol for any argument; use Walton's scheme-specific critical questions when the argument type has been identified to apply more targeted evaluation.

delphi_analysis_skill.relationship_type: Elaboration of Detecting and Analyzing Arguments
delphi_analysis_skill.description: The Delphi Report's Analysis skill includes 'Detecting Arguments' and 'Analyzing Arguments' — identifying inferential structures and patterns of reasoning. Walton's schemes are the catalog of those inferential patterns, each precisely specified with its critical questions. A student who has internalized both frameworks can identify an argument's presence (Delphi Analysis), classify it by type (Walton scheme), and evaluate it against the appropriate standards (Walton critical questions).
delphi_analysis_skill.key_connection: Walton's argumentation schemes are the detailed implementation of Delphi's Analysis skill at the level of real-world argument types. Where Delphi specifies that arguments should be analyzed, Walton specifies exactly how.
